summary: The note describes the British one pound coin, which has two versions in circulation since 28 March 2017: the original round coin and a new 12-sided bimetallic coin with a hidden security feature called iSIS, introduced to counter counterfeiting. It also covers the coin's design, including its obverse inscriptions and Queen Elizabeth II portraits, and the reverse emblems of the four UK nations on the 2017 coin.
one_line: Overview of the British one pound coin, its 2017 dodecagonal redesign with the iSIS security feature, and its design history.
key_facts: Since 28 March 2017, two versions of the one pound coin have been in circulation: the original round design and a new dodecagonal (12-sided) design.
As of March 2014 there were an estimated 1,553 million round £1 coins in circulation.
The Royal Mint estimated in 2014 that 3.04% (about 47 million) of round £1 coins were counterfeit.
The new 12-sided £1 coin is bimetallic, like the current £2 coin.
The new 12-sided coin features an undisclosed hidden security feature called 'iSIS' (Integrated Secure Identification Systems).
The round pound will remain in circulation until 15 October 2017.
After 15 October 2017, the older round coin can only be redeemed at banks.
The British one pound (£1) coin is a denomination of the pound sterling.
The obverse of the coin bears the Latin engraving DG REG, meaning 'By the grace of God, Queen'.
The obverse also bears the letters FD, meaning Fidei defensor, Defender of the Faith.
The one pound coin has featured the profile of Queen Elizabeth II since its introduction on 21 April 1983.
Four different portraits of the Queen have been used on the coin.
The latest portrait, by Jody Clark, was introduced in 2015.
The reverse of the new 2017 coin features four emblems representing the nations of the United Kingdom.
The four emblems are the English rose, the leek for Wales, the Scottish thistle, and the shamrock for Northern Ireland, emerging from a single stem within a crown.
